Bayesian noisy-channel belief updating model captures the timecourse of eyegaze during speech perception

The posterior distribution of this best-fitting model is summarized in Figure 4C-D.

To summarize the results, I report means (M ) of the posterior samples as point estimates of conditions or differences (∆) between conditions along with 95% posterior credible intervals (95% CrI) of those estimates.

Across conditions and blocks, the model predicts that fixations to the target increase as the stimulus unfolds (t0: M = 0.30, 95% CrI = [0.28, 0.31]; t1: M = 0.46, 95% CrI = [0.45, 0.48]; t2: M = 0.65, 95% CrI = [0.63, 0.67]; t3: M = 0.73, 95% CrI = [0.72, 0.75]).

Fixations to the competitor in the Early competition condition are higher early and decrease in the third and fourth time windows (t0: M = 0.27, 95% CrI = [0.25, 0.30]; t1: M = 0.28, 95% CrI = [0.25, 0.30]; t2: M = 0.18, 95% CrI = [0.15, 0.20]; t3: M = 0.14, 95% CrI = [0.12, 0.16]), while those in the Late competition condition remain elevated in the latest time window (t0: M = 0.25, 95% CrI = [0.23, 0.27]; t1: M = 0.22, 95% CrI = [0.20, 0.25]; t2: M = 0.20, 95% CrI = [0.18, 0.22]; t3: M = 0.18, 95% CrI = [0.16, 0.21]).

To quantify how much competitors capture attention in different conditions and time windows, I calculate the posterior estimate of the target advantage as the proportion of fixations to the target minus the proportion of fixations to the competitor or one of the distractors. Greater target advantage indicates more attention to the target relative to the competitor or distractor (i.e., less competition). Across conditions and blocks, the model predicts that the target advantage increases as the stimulus unfolded (t0: M = 0.04, 95% CrI = [0.01, 0.06]; t1: M = 0.24, 95% CrI = [0.21, 0.26]; t2: M = 0.49, 95% CrI = [0.46, 0.52]; t3: M = 0.60, 95% CrI = [0.57, 0.62]). In the pre-noun onset time window (t0), the target advantage does not differ by condition (∆ Early -No Compet. = -0.04, 95% CrI Early -No Compet. = [-0.10, 0.02], ∆ Late -No Compet. = -0.01, 95% CrI Late -No Compet. = [-0.07, 0.05]). In the second time window (t1), the target advantage is more likely to be larger in the No Competition condition than in the Early competition condition (∆ Early -No Compet. = -0.17, 95% CrI Early -No Compet. = [-0.23, -0.10] ) or the Late Competition condition (∆ Late -No Compet. = -0.08, 95% CrI Late -No Compet. = [-0.14, -0.02]), indicating competition from both early and late competitors in this window. The target advantage was reduced in the Early Competition condition relative to the Late Competition condition (∆ Early -Late = -0.08, 95% CrI Early -Late = [-0.15, -0.02]), indicating greater competition from the early competitors in this window. In the third time window (t2), the target advantage is more likely to be larger in the No Competition condition than in the Early competition condition (∆ Early -No Compet. = -0.13, 95% CrI Early -No Compet. = [-0.19, -0.08] ) or the Late Competition condition (∆ Late -No Compet. = -0.18, 95% CrI Late -No Compet. = [-0.23, -0.12]). The target advantage was nominally increased in the Early Competition condition relative to the Late Competition condition (∆ Early -Late = 0.04, 95% CrI Early -Late = [-0.02, 0.11]), indicating similar competition from the early and late competitors in this window. Finally, in the fourth time window (t3), the target advantage is more likely to be greater in the No Competition condition than in the Early competition condition (∆ Early -No Compet. = -0.12, 95% CrI Early -No Compet. = [-0.18, -0.07]) and the Late Competition condition (∆ Late -No Compet. = -0.20, 95% CrI Late -No Compet. = [-0.26, -0.15]). The target advantage was increased in the Early Competition condition relative to the Late Competition condition (∆ Early -Late = 0.08, 95% CrI Early -Late = [0.02, 0.14]), indicating greater competition from the late competitors in this window.

In sum, the posterior estimates capture the critical patterns observed in the eye-tracking data (Figure 4E).

Listeners adapt to the noise in the environment

In addition to demonstrating that the competition condition effects are well captured by a Bayesian noisy-channel model, analysis of the posterior reveals that listeners adapt their estimate of the noise probability, τ , in response to the noise in the environment, based on multiple sources of information. Figure 5A summarizes the posterior predictions of the timecourse of fixation proportions to targets and competitors across competition conditions, comparing all Intact blocks and Noisy blocks. Added noise in fillers decreases fixations to the target across competition conditions suggesting that τ is lower in the Intact blocks.

The posterior estimates of τ values by block type and contrasts between blocks are summarized in Figures 5B and C. The lowest τ is observed in the first Intact block which did not contain added noise on filler trials (M = 0.082, 95% CrI = [0.079, 0.086]). The highest τ is observed in the first Noisy block (M = 0.104, 95% CrI = [0.099, 0.109], ∆ = 0.022, 95% CrI = [0.016, 0.028]), indicating that listeners increase their noise estimates when there is an elevated frequency of acoustic noise in their environment. τ was higher for the Intact block when it was preceded by a Noisy block (M = 0.094, 95% CrI = [0.090, 0.098], ∆ = 0.012, 95% CrI = [0.007, 0.017]) suggesting that the estimate of noise is based on continuous perceptual evidence accumulation. Similarly, τ was lower for the Noisy block when it was preceded by an Intact block (M = 0.091, 95% CrI = [0.086, 0.095], ∆ = -0.013, 95% CrI = [-0.020, -0.007]). Finally, τ was lower for the Intact block preceded by a Noisy block if the participant was explicitly informed that there was an error in the previous block and that the following set of stimuli would not contain acoustic noise (M = 0.087, 95% CrI = [0.084, 0.091], ∆ = -0.007, 95% CrI = [-0.012, -0.001]). In addition to accumulating perceptual evidence, listeners can also flexibly update their noise estimates based on a verbal characterization, which "explains away" the presence of noise.

Discussion

The present findings demonstrate that the timecourse of eye-gaze during spoken word comprehension is well-modeled as noisy-channel inference continuously and incrementally unfolding in real time. The representational geometry of (late) Transformer layers in Hu-BERT captures, at least in part, the listener's noise model, allowing for fine-grained quantitative predictions of gaze behavior and providing a window into the nature of representations in HuBERT (de Heer Kloots et al., 2026; Pasad, Shi, & Livescu, 2023). Model comparison results indicated that a noise model with stimulus-specific representational geometry did not improve eye-gaze prediction over a generic noise likelihood (shared across all stimuli). One possibility is that this reflects a noise model in the human mind that is fairly coarse-grained.

Alternatively, the deep speech model representations may be too noisy to capture the finegrained acoustic distinctions in the minds of human listeners. Relatedly, the stimuli used in the current dataset may not sufficiently span the similarity space to reveal the predictive benefit of stimulus-specific noise likelihoods. Further probing of HuBERT representations, and comparison with other models, may be fruitful in revealing the structure of the noise model.

Crucially, the noise model is adaptive. The fitted uncertainty parameter τ was higher during blocks in which acoustic noise was added to the fillers, indicating that the probability of noise in the listener's mind is malleable and tuned to the statistics of noise in the environment (consistent with findings from McQueen & Huettig, 2012). Furthermore, when the noise was reduced and participants were explicitly told that the stimuli would have less noise than what came before, τ was lower than if they were not told, indicating that the probability of noise may be updated by multiple routes: both implicit perceptual evidence accumulation and explicit re-structuring of a causal model of the environment.

These results are consistent with recent findings that acoustic-phonetic adaptation involves incremental, "associative-like" learning (N. D. Anderson, Holmes, Dell, & Middleton, 2019) as well as causal inferences about the sources of variation in the input (Denby & Goldrick, 2021; Liu & Jaeger, 2018; but see Liu & Jaeger, 2019).

The model presented here can be refined in future work in a number of ways. For instance, in its current form, the model over-predicts fixations to the target in the second time window. This may be due to temporal misalignment and averaging. Currently, eye gaze time windows are offset by 200ms-a standard estimate of oculomotor delay-relative to the audio, but a slightly longer offset may be more appropriate. Fitting a more fine-grained timecourse (e.g., 20ms bins) may provide a more accurate characterization of the temporal dynamics of gaze. The model also slightly over-predicts fixations to the competitor with late overlap. Speculatively, this may be related to the weight placed on sequence endings by the dynamic time warping algorithm, suggesting that this algorithm may deviate in important ways from the way that similarity between acoustic sequences is computed in the mind.

Further, the level of uncertainty (τ ) is currently tied to the experiment block. In reality this τ value is likely to be dynamically updated on a more fine-grained timescale-changing from trial to trial or even moment-by-moment as a word unfolds.

These results extend the Noisy Channel framework to real-time spoken language comprehension and suggest an avenue for investigating how additional information sources (e.g., semantic, syntactic, pragmatic) are integrated moment-by-moment during noisy-channel comprehension. This account has the potential to explain other existing observations in the speech comprehension literature. For example, as demonstrated by Norris and McQueen (2008), the presence of frequency effects in eye-gaze (i.e., higher frequency competitors elicit more fixations than low frequency competitors in an eye-tracking setup similar to the one used here, Dahan, Magnuson, & Tanenhaus, 2001) is straightforwardly accommodated by changing the prior (at the first timestep) to reflect the relative frequencies of the candidate referents in the language.foot_0 Further, anadrome effects (i.e., anadromes of target words like "sub" to "bus" elicit more fixations than competitors with overlapping sounds like "sun, " Toscano, Anderson, & McMurray, 2013) may reflect the listener's expectation that a speaker intending to say "bus" is more likely to produce a speech error resulting in "sub"

than "sun". I leave a test of this hypothesis to future work. The approach taken here also opens the door to discovering how noisy-channel inference is implemented in the brain by connecting moment-by-moment predictions to the neural timecourse of speech processing (e.g., Gwilliams, Linzen, Poeppel, & Marantz, 2018).

More broadly, this account points to a view of language comprehension and processing as inference over a generative model of the communication process, including the speaker's intention to produce an utterance and multiple potential sources of corruption during transmission (e.g., speech errors, attention or memory lapses, Ryskin, Poliak et al., 2026). The utility of using speech model representational geometry to capture listeners' real-time inferences, as demonstrated here, opens the door to further fine-grained investigations of the information contained in the noise model of human comprehenders, as well as the evaluation of artificial speech models on their ability to mirror the rich temporal dynamics of human perception.

Methods

All pre-processed data are available on OSF (https://osf.io/ybxru/overview?view_only=33cb61764a7c4d7baa8fdbb5b28cd1f3) and the code to reproduce the manuscript is available at: https://github.com/raryskin/noisy-channel-speech. Google's Gemini large language model and Anthropic's Claude (Opus 5.5) were used for assistance with code generation and debugging.

Eye-tracking experiment

Participants. 96 students at the University of California, Merced participated in the eye-tracking experiment in exchange for course credit, after providing informed consent.

All reported having normal or corrected-to-normal vision. One additional participant's data were excluded because their accuracy on filler trials was below 90%.

Procedure. Participants sat in front of a computer display with four pictures of objects, listened to instructions of the form "Click on the <referent>," and used the mouse to respond. Their eye movements were recorded by an Eyelink-1000 Plus desktop eyetracker (with chin rest) from SR Research sampling at 1000 Hz, after a 9-point calibration and validation. Drift checks were included after each trial. Participants were told that there were two sets of instructions and pictures and that they would get a break after the first set. The session began with 3 practice trials, followed by Trial condition was manipulated within participants and items. Block Order condition was manipulated between participants. Which items appeared in which block was randomly counterbalanced across participants. The order of trials within a block and the location of images on each trial were randomly generated on-the-fly for each participant using the PsychoPy library for stimulus presentation (Peirce et al., 2019).

Competition Condition.

24 sets of stimuli were created (see example in Table 1), corresponding to a target word (e.g., "beaker"), a competitor with early acoustic overlap ("beetle"), a competitor with late acoustic overlap ("speaker"), and several distractor words (e.g., "apple"). The item sets were chosen using the LexFindR package (Li, Crinnion, & Magnuson, 2022) so that the words comprising each set were similar in frequency.

Appropriate visual stimuli were then selected from a larger set of normed pictures used in previous eye-tracking studies. Each set included 3 critical competition conditions as well as 3 filler conditions. For all 3 critical trials, the audio instruction referred to the target word (e.g., "Click on the beaker"). In the No competition condition, there were no competitors in the display. In the Early competition condition, the set of images included a competitor with early acoustic overlap. In the Late competition condition, the set of images included a competitor with late acoustic overlap. In the Filler 1 condition, the audio instruction referred to the early competitor (e.g., "Click on the beetle"). In the Filler 2 condition, the audio instruction referred to the late competitor (e.g., "Click on the speaker"). In the Filler 3 condition, the audio instruction referred to a distractor. The fillers were meant to ensure that participants couldn't predict which image they would need to click on simply by seeing the set of images.

Each item set appeared in all 3 critical trial conditions, as well as all 3 filler conditions within a block. 12 item sets were presented in each block. Which 12 item/stimulus sets participants received in the first vs. the second block was randomly counterbalanced across participants.

Block Condition.

Each participant received two blocks. There were 72 trials (36 critical and 36 filler) in each block. For a given participant, one block was assigned to the Intact condition and one block was assigned to the Noisy condition. 3 In the Noisy condition, two-thirds of the filler trial instructions contain added acoustic noise in the form of white noise or radio noise spliced into one or two sections of the preamble (e.g., "Click #n the apple", in different randomly chosen locations across items), the beginning of the referent ("Click on the #pple"), the middle of the referent ("Click on the a#le"), or the end of the referent ("Click on the appl#"). Of the noisy fillers, two-thirds had only one noise corruption spliced in and one-third had two. In order to create the noisy versions of the filler audio files, 3 The eye-tracking experiment was inspired by a previous study by McQueen and Huettig (2012), but the paradigm was changed in several important ways. McQueen and Huettig (2012) used a passive listening and viewing task and targets were not present on the screen, meaning that the listener's goal was not to infer the referent given the spoken input. (It also meant they only analyzed fixations to the competitors.) The noise manipulation in their study was between subjects and the added noise was always in the same position, either the beginning of a word or the middle (position manipulated between subjects).

several audio files with different kinds of noise were obtained from the web and were spliced into the clean audio files (see details below). The position of the noise was uniformly distributed across items such that when noise might appear wouldn't be predictable to listeners. In the Intact condition, none of the fillers contained any acoustic noise. In both block conditions, the critical trials never contained acoustic noise. 25 participants first heard the Intact block. For participants who first heard the Noisy block followed by the Intact block, one group received no explanation before the start of the second block, and the other group received an explanation. When no explanation was given (N=34), participants were simply told to take a break before starting the second half. When an explanation was presented (N=37), participants saw an "error message" after the first block ended: "FATAL ERROR: Audio files corrupted." This prompted the participant to alert the experimenter, who apologized and explained that the wrong files had been used. The experimenter then initiated the second block, explicitly noting that the 'correct,' corruption-free audio files had now been loaded.

Audio stimuli and embeddings

The audio stimuli were created using text-to-speech software, specifically the macOS say command-line utility. This yielded audio stimuli that were clear and intelligible but readily recognizable as synthetic-a deliberate choice to make the subsequent noise manipulations seem like plausible corruptions resulting from the same generative process. Noisy versions of filler audio stimuli were created by replacing segments of the audio file with segments of noise that were equal in duration using Praat software for speech analysis (Boersma & Weenink, 2022). Noise consisted of a mix of static noise and radio noise downloaded from freesound.org. Praat was also used to annotate the 4 time windows of interest on critical trials: 1) t 0 : from the start of the audio file to the onset of the critical word (e.g., beaker), 2) t 1 : from the onset of the critical word to the onset of the phoneme which disambiguates the target word from the cohort competitor (e.g., "k" for beaker -beetle), 3) t 2 : from the onset of the disambiguating phoneme to the offset of the disambiguating phoneme, and 4) t 3 : from the offset of the disambiguating phoneme to the end of the word.

In addition to audio files that were used as the stimuli for the experiment, audio files corresponding to all other images presented during the experiment were generated by the same procedure. These were used to derive similarities between the acoustic information of the spoken input and the acoustic information of possible alternative referents.

Embeddings for every audio file were extracted from the pre-trained HuBERT extra large model fine-tuned on automatic speech recognition (hubert-xlarge-ls960-ft) using the transformers library from HuggingFace (Wolf et al., 2020). HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021) was chosen because it has been shown to capture human perceptual judgments (Chernyak, Bradlow, Keshet, & Goldrick, 2024; Nguyen, Sagot, & Dupoux, 2022). For each audio file, forward passes were performed on an incrementally increasing number of frames until the end of the audio file was reached, and embeddings were extracted from the last frame of each forward pass. This ensures that the embeddings for a given frame do not reflect any information from later in the audio. This generated a 1280-dimensional embedding for each 20ms frame of the audio from each of the 48 transformer layers. Dynamic time warping, implemented via the librosa package (McFee et al., 2025), was used to generate alignments between every pair of audio files. Frame-by-frame cosine similarity was calculated on the aligned timecourses using the frame numbers of the target audio file as reference.

Similarities were then averaged within the 4 time windows of interest separately for each layer. Self-similarity (i.e., target-target similarity) was set to 1 -10 -7.

Eye-tracking data pre-processing

The x and y coordinates of participants' gaze were continuously recorded during each trial of the experiment. Eye gaze data were pre-processed and analyzed using custom R scripts. Only trials in which participants correctly clicked on the target were included.

Each fixation was categorized in terms of whether it fell into one of the four regions of interest (ROI): the four quadrants of the display. In order to visualize the full timecourse of eye-gaze during word recognition, fixations were timelocked to the onset of the critical word in the audio instruction (e.g., "beaker"). A binary fixation measure for each ROI was computed for every 10ms bin, starting 200ms before the onset of the critical word and ending 2s after the onset of the critical word. For analysis, fixation durations were calculated per trial for each ROI in four time windows of interest, reflecting how much total time was spent on each of the ROIs within that time window per trial. These were then converted to proportions by dividing each ROI's duration by the summed total duration across all ROIs. The four time windows of interest were determined by critical moments in the audio stimulus (detailed above) and were offset by 200ms to account for oculomotor delay.

Trials with poor tracking quality were defined as those in which a fixation to any one of the 4 ROIs was recorded in fewer than 50% of the 10ms timebins. These trials were removed before analysis or visualization. This affected 1.70% of trials. Proportion of low track quality trials per participant ranged from 0% to 26.40%.

Modeling

To estimate τ values from the eye-tracking data, the Bayesian belief updating model was implemented in Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017). Sampling was done using the cmdstanr interface (Gabry, Češnovar, Johnson, & Bronder, 2025). Fixation duration proportions were averaged across subjects and trial orders resulting in a 4-dimensional vector of average fixation duration proportions for each item in each block type per time window. These average fixation duration proportions were then transformed to prevent values of exactly 1 or 0 while ensuring that they summed to 1. This allowed the allocation of gaze to the 4 ROIs to be modeled using a Dirichlet distribution. Sampling was run using 4 MCMC chains for 2000 iterations (1000 discarded for warm-up). R values were 1.00 for all parameters and there were no divergent transitions. Weakly informative priors were used for the concentration parameter of the Dirichlet distribution (log(ϕ) ∼ N ormal(log(50), 1)) and the noise parameter (log(τ ) ∼ N ormal(0, 1)). framework to Roger Levy, Ted Gibson, Moshe Poliak, Thomas Clark, Peng Qian, and Sihan Chen. Figure 1.

Figure1. Illustration of incremental "noisy-channel" speech perception. A) The speaker and the listener see a table with a beaker, a beetle, an apple, and an audio speaker. The person speaking aims to refer to the beaker. Left: The listener has heard only the beginning of the word. The prior probability that the person speaking would have referred to any of the four objects is equivalent. The noise likelihood assigns greater probability to the input given the beaker and beetle referents than given the speaker and apple referents. According to Bayes' rule, the resulting posterior probabilities for the beaker and the beetle are higher than for the speaker and the apple. Right: The listener has heard the rest of the word. The prior probability is the posterior from the previous timestep. The noise likelihood assigns greater probability to the input given the beaker and speaker referents than given the beetle and apple referents. The resulting posterior probability for the beaker is highest but posterior probabilities for the beetle and the speaker are both higher than for the apple. B) The likelihood is proposed to be modulated by a noise/uncertainty parameter, τ (arbitrary "high" and "low" values chosen for visualization). Higher assumed noise (larger τ ) flattens the distribution, pulling the probabilities of an acoustic input given different referents closer to uniform. C) Idealized posterior predictions across four timesteps and the effect of τ . At the first timestep, before the onset of the noun, the posterior probability, P (r i | s) is equal for all four possible referents because they are equally likely to be referred to a priori (P (r i ) = .25) and the probability of saying "Click on the. . . " is also equally high for all possible referents (set to P (s | r i ) = .99 in this simulation). At the second timestep, the priors for referents are taken from the posteriors at the previous timestep. The listener hears /'bi:/, so the probability of the input given the beaker and beetle referents is equally high (e.g., P (s = /'bi:/ | r = beaker) = P (s = /'bi:/ | r = beetle) = .9 for low noise), whereas the probability of the utterance given the other two possible referents is very low (e.g., P (s = /'bi:/ | r = speaker) = .1). At the third timestep, the listener hears /k/, so the probability of the input given the beaker and speaker referents is equally high (e.g., P (s = /k/ | r = beaker) = .9), whereas the probability of the utterance given the other two possible referents is very low (e.g., P (s = /k/ | r = beetle) = .1). At the last timestep, the listener hears "er," so again the probability of the utterance given the beaker and speaker referents is equally high (e.g., P (s = /er/ | r = beaker) = .9), whereas the probability of the utterance given the other two possible referents is very low (e.g., P (s = /er/ | r = beetle) = .1). When there is more noise overall (higher τ ), there is more uncertainty in the posterior over referents at each timestep.
